findings.description: Regular expression pattern vulnerable to ReDoS via repetition of group with quantifier
findings.code_snippet: return re.sub(r"(%[a-f0-9]{2})+", repl_func, string, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
findings.reasoning: The pattern `(%[a-f0-9]{2})+` uses a quantified group with a `+` operator. This creates exponential backtracking when the regex engine tries to match malformed input like a long string of `%` characters not followed by exactly 2 hex digits. The engine will try different combinations of matching/not matching the inner group, leading to catastrophic backtracking. For example, an input like `%` repeated thousands of times will cause the regex engine to spend exponential time attempting to match.

evidence.code_context: The decode function uses re.sub() with the pattern r"(%[a-f0-9]{2})+" to process URL-encoded strings. The pattern expects percent-encoded characters (% followed by exactly 2 hex digits), repeated one or more times.
evidence.dataflow_analysis: The vulnerable pattern is used in re.sub() at line 36, which is called with user-controlled string input from the 'string' parameter. An attacker can pass a malformed string to trigger ReDoS.
evidence.notes: The pattern has nested quantification: the group (...) has a quantifier + applied to it. When input fails to match fully, the regex engine backtracks exponentially trying different combinations of whether each group instance matched or not.

findings.description: Regular expression pattern vulnerable to ReDoS with overlapping character classes
findings.code_snippet: if slashes_denote_host or proto or re.search(r"^//[^@/]+@[^@/]+", rest):
findings.reasoning: The pattern `^//[^@/]+@[^@/]+` uses character class negation with repetition. The `[^@/]+` quantifier can cause catastrophic backtracking when applied to input like `//aaaaaa...` (without an @ character). The regex engine will try many combinations of where to split the characters between the two `[^@/]+` parts before giving up. This is a classic ReDoS pattern with overlapping character classes.

evidence.code_context: The pattern is used in re.search() at line 146 in the parse() method to check if a URL contains a user@host pattern in the protocol-relative URL form (//user@host).
evidence.dataflow_analysis: The vulnerable regex is applied to the 'rest' variable which contains the remaining part of the URL string after protocol extraction. This can come from user input through the parse() method.
evidence.notes: The pattern uses [^@/]+ twice with an @ in between. When the input has many characters that match [^@/] but no @ character, the regex engine will try exponential combinations to match the two separate [^@/]+ sequences before failing.

findings.description: Regular expression pattern vulnerable to ReDoS with repeated character class and quantifier
findings.code_snippet: PROTOCOL_PATTERN = re.compile(r"^([a-z0-9.+-]+:)", flags=re.IGNORECASE)
findings.reasoning: The pattern `^([a-z0-9.+-]+:)` has a character class `[a-z0-9.+-]` with the `+` quantifier. The `+` character itself is within the character class and also used as a quantifier on the class, creating potential for backtracking. When given input like a long string of `+` or `.` characters not followed by `:`, the regex engine will try many combinations to match the character class before failing.

evidence.notes: The character class [a-z0-9.+-] contains special characters including + which could cause ambiguity. The + quantifier applied to this class means one or more of these characters followed by a colon.

findings.description: Regular expression pattern vulnerable to ReDoS with complex alternation and character classes
findings.code_snippet: SIMPLE_PATH_PATTERN = re.compile(r"^(//?(?!/)[^?\s]*)(\\?[^\\s]*)?$")
findings.reasoning: The pattern `^(//?(?!/)[^?\s]*)(\\?[^\\s]*)?$` has multiple components that can cause backtracking. The `[^?\s]*` quantifier combined with the negative lookahead `(?!/)` and the optional group `(...)?` at the end creates multiple ways the regex engine can match the input. Input with many characters that could match `[^?\s]*` but fail at the end can cause exponential backtracking.

evidence.notes: The pattern has [^?\s]* which can match any number of characters that aren't ? or whitespace, combined with optional group (\?[^\s]*)? at the end. This creates multiple possible matching paths for the same input.

findings.description: Regular expression pattern vulnerable to ReDoS with capture group and greedy matching
findings.code_snippet: HOSTNAME_PART_START = re.compile(r"^([+a-z0-9A-Z_-]{0,63})(.*)$")

While the first group is bounded to 63 characters, the `.*` can match anything and creates potential for backtracking when combined with the alternation in the character class. The pattern splits a hostname part and the rest of the input, and malformed input could cause backtracking.

findings.description: False positive: Function parse has implicit input validation through regex pattern matching and string operations
findings.code_snippet:
def parse(self, url: str, slashes_denote_host: bool) -> "MutableURL":
        lower_proto = ""
        slashes = False
        rest = url

        # trim before proceeding.
        # This is to support parse stuff like "  http://foo.com  \n"
        rest = rest.strip()

        if not slashes_denote_host and len(url.split("#")) == 1:
            # Try fast path regexp
            simple_path = SIMPLE_PATH_PATTERN.match(rest)
            if simple_path:
                self.pathname = simple_path.group(1)
                if simple_path.group(2):
                    self.search = simple_path.group(2)
                return self

        proto = ""
        proto_match = PROTOCOL_PATTERN.match(rest)
        if proto_match:
            proto = proto_match.group()
            lower_proto = proto.lower()
            self.protocol = proto
            rest = rest[len(proto) :]
findings.reasoning: The 'url' parameter is validated implicitly through: (1) .strip() to handle whitespace, (2) regex pattern matching with PROTOCOL_PATTERN and SIMPLE_PATH_PATTERN which validate URL structure, (3) .split() and string slicing with safe bounds. The 'slashes_denote_host' parameter is a boolean with implicit type validation. The function safely processes arbitrary URL strings through regex-based validation.
